title: The hungry ghosts
hookLine: in Chinese communities, the seventh month's offerings to hungry ghosts and lost souls

cards: Singapore, the seventh month of the lunar calendar. On the sidewalks, small fires burn in metal bins, paper offerings curling into ash. Little piles of oranges, rice and incense sit along the curbs.
In open-air tents, singers perform loud, cheerful shows, and the front row of seats is left empty. Those seats, people say, are for the guests you can't see.
Yesterday, Moggallana's mother was one hungry ghost, and her son could help her. In Chinese communities, this whole month is for all the others: the ghosts nobody remembers.

teach.b: In Buddhist teaching, hungry ghosts, peta in Pali, preta in Sanskrit, are one of the realms of rebirth: beings driven by craving so strong that nothing satisfies it.
East Asian art pictures them with huge, empty bellies and throats as thin as a needle, always hungry, never able to swallow enough. Craving, made visible. The Pali canon already speaks of them.
A short text, the discourse outside the walls, pictures dead relatives standing outside houses, at crossroads and by doorposts, returning to their old homes, waiting.
When the living give food and drink and dedicate the merit to them, the ghosts rejoice. In China, these threads came together with older customs of honoring the dead.
On the fifteenth night of the seventh month, Buddhist temples hold the Ullambana rites you heard about yesterday; Taoists keep the same night as the Zhongyuan festival.
Often the two are woven together, and families may not draw a sharp line.
In some temples, monks perform a ritual of feeding the hungry ghosts, scattering food and chanting so that it can reach beings who can't otherwise eat. Notice who the month is really for.
Not only your own grandparents: the lost ones, who died far from home or with no one left to remember them. The festival is a public kindness toward strangers who can't say thank you.

how: In Chinese communities during the seventh lunar month, families make offerings of food, incense and paper goods, temples hold rites to feed hungry ghosts, and some communities stage performances with front-row seats left empty for unseen guests.

games.q: it's the seventh month. there's a show in an open tent, and the front row is empty. what do you do?
o: leave the front row empty, for the unseen guests.
ask the organizers to fill it.
games.why: by custom, the front row is left for the ghosts. it's a quiet courtesy to those nobody else remembers.

practice: First, notice hunger in yourself, any kind: for food, for attention, for something to be different, and see it without judging, like the ghost's thin throat.
Then widen out to the hungry people near you: a shelter, a person on a corner, a neighbor stretched thin. Hold them a while, and wish them fed.

wordCard.voice: peta. The Pali word for a departed one, a hungry ghost, a being whose craving can never be satisfied, fed with offerings in the seventh lunar month in Chinese communities. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali peta (Sanskrit preta): 'departed one,' a hungry ghost, one of the realms of rebirth.

carryVoice: Your line: feed the hungry. Even the ones nobody remembers. That's six hundred eighty-seven days.
